speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Mr Chairman, I beg to move, "That the total sum to be allocated for Head M of the Estimates be reduced by $100".

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Mr Chairman, one of the key thrusts of this year's Budget is about ensuring fiscal prudence and sustainability: how do we manage rising expenditures and how do we find the revenue to fund this spending in the years ahead.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is a full plate for the Ministry of Finance (MOF).

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: These across-the-board measures are necessary to instill prudence and discipline in spending.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It would internalise cost consciousness among the Government agencies and would have an overall financial impact when aggregated across the scale of the Government.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The natural follow-up question to ask is whether, with these measures in place, would the agencies go overzealous in cost management and, as a result, impact service delivery or to look to increase fees?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Would these downward adjustments to Budget caps have an impact on planned investments by Ministries and agencies which have wanted to enhance and upgrade their systems to improve efficiency and effectiveness but would now have to shelve their plans due to Budget caps?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: While we should be extremely prudent in our spending, we know that there can be no goodness achieved by just mindlessly cutting costs.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Rather, we should look to more work-smart initiatives, processes and workflow improvements and, importantly, cutting unnecessary red tape as among the areas of focus to manage costs and improve service delivery.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, I like this mantra "value-for-money" often propagated by MOF.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It needs no explanation and this is a better attitude to take when we review projects rather than to just say no to all spending increases.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As I said during the Budget Debate, between not spending on needed essential items or cutting spending, I rather the Government spend prudently but look for more revenue sources so that we continue to provide more to improve the quality of life of our people.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Mr Chairman, beyond managing efficiency within the Government, we can and should also encourage and empower ground agencies to seek local innovative solutions to local problems where we can and it can also achieve the value-for-money principle.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Allow me to relate a real-life example of how an enlightened decision by a secondary school principal in my constituency can achieve a "value-for-no money" outcome for the Government and yet is a win-win situation for all.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In my constituency's Senja Estate, the Housing and Development Board (HDB) is now constructing a cluster of Build-To-Order (BTO) flats known as Senja Ridges.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The site of the BTO is immediately adjacent to West Spring Secondary School and, as Members can imagine, the construction noises will cause tremendous noise nuisance to the students studying there.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Hence, as part of the contractual arrangements, the contractor is required to build a high wall in the narrow spaces between the school and the BTO site to block off some of the noises and minimise the impact.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Of course, this may well be an intuitive solution to the problem which may partially reduce the construction noise, but it would also mean that the overall ambience of school will be affected.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Imagine students looking out of their classroom windows, only to be greeted by the high walls, the boring walls, staring at them.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Moreover, the wall will also not come cheap for the contractor as it needs to be strong enough to withstand the vibrations of the construction site.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, the school and the contractor met up to discuss the project.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As a result, students now can study in the comfort of an air-conditioned environment which is an even more effective way to block out the construction noises than compared to the wall.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: From the contractor's standpoint, they do not need to build a high wall and would not need to have to demolish the wall when the BTO project is completed, which I presume, the total costs will be more than the installation of the air-conditioning.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, here we have an "out-of-the-box" solution which is a win-win for everyone.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We should encourage more of such creative and smart ideas to solve local problems and tap on the power of ground-up ingenuity to get the solution out to solve local problems.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The last thing we want is to have a stifling environment within the whole-of-Government system such that good ideas and solutions do not get to see the light of day.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Chairman, Sir, my apology for the hoarseness in my voice.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: It is critical that we consider our expenditure growth very carefully and take every step to ensure we get the best value for the money we spend.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: In the private sector, it is a common strategy to consider cost cutting in other areas to fund new investments and increases in expenditures.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: I call on the Government to take a bottom-up analysis of each Ministry's expenditure needs and scrutinise and prioritise cost items.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The Finance Minister has introduced the discipline of moderating the pace of the Ministries' Budget growth in the last two Budgets.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: What more can the Government do to work smarter and more efficiently?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: First, I would like to ask the Minister if the operations of Ministries and Statutory Boards are subject to productivity reviews to establish their operational efficiency and goals for improvement.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Given the vast number of agencies in operation, Ministries can leverage off such reviews to establish best practices and improve their processes to become leaner.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: How will public officers be rewarded for cost savings they manage to secure against the allocated Budget for projects?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: There should be incentives to recognise public officers' efforts and cost savings.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: We do hear of stories of public sector officers rushing to spend allocated funds toward the end of the financial year, about this time, often on programmes they could have done without.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The understanding is that they fear being penalised in future Budgets if they under-utilise the current Budget.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Third, with increasingly complex challenges facing the Government, it is critical that the public sector agencies adopt a coordinated whole-of-Government response and work collaboratively to avoid duplication of efforts and costs.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: I am pleased that the recent Public Sector (Governance) Bill sends a strong signal on the importance of cross-agency coordination.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: I believe that much cost synergies may be realised from cross-agency collaboration and interagency sharing of data.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Chairman, Sir, back in 2008, the Government Investment Corporation (GIC) was part of the pioneering effort to develop the Santiago Principles, a common global set of 24 voluntary guidelines that assign best practices for the operations of Sovereign Wealth Funds (SWFs).

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: These principles address concerns about visibility, accountability and the governing structure of SWFs, and include ethics and professionalism in the ability to follow foreign rules.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Though Temasek does not direct business decisions or operations in its portfolio companies, it pitches itself as an active promoter of sound corporate governance in them.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As a sole shareholder of Temasek, the Government should naturally be concerned that the entities in Temasek invest and adhere to the spirit of the Santiago Principles in order to safeguard Singapore's Reserves and international reputation.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Turning to what other countries have done, the Norwegian Government Pension Fund Global has led the way.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Through an ethics council established in 2004, companies that are unethical are excluded from its investment portfolio.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It appointed a corporate governance advisory board in 2013 to be a more engaged and more responsible investor.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Oil Fund has tackled issues, such as high executive pay, by voting against pay proposals at Alphabet JP Morgan and Volkswagen in 2017.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: While the Santiago Principles require that SWFs like Temasek be operationally independent from their owners, that is, MOF, how has MOF worked with Temasek on areas, such as its investment policies or otherwise, to maintain ethics?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Will MOF add further accountability for Temasek on the ethics front?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I am of the view that reputational challenges to Singapore’s integrity as a country should not be left to be steered by what is legally just a commercial entity.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Or are Temasek and GIC totally hands off, as it were?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Are they not interfering in investment business decisions or operations at all?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Not even offering insights, information or suggestions of any kind on any matter, be it commercial or corporate governance-related?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Azmoon Ahmad, you can take the two cuts together

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: While there is no hard and fast rule on how a surplus is to be distributed or what and where it should be allocated to, I would like to mention that the proportion is highly skewed towards savings for the future.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: If my calculations are correct, about 72% of the total surplus is being saved which means $5 billion plus $1.9 billion over the $9.6 billion.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: I do support saving but I thought this matter is worth mentioning.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: I think that the distribution is highly lopsided on the savings side.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: What model should we adopt when there are surpluses?

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: How can we arrive at a distribution model which serves the interests of the now, the near future and the future?

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Should we not derive a baseline where the distribution and allocation models are acceptable, just like our Net Investment Returns (NIR)?

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: These suggestions or views should not be the only ones considered.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: They can serve as an exercise to get a discussion going to arrive at a baseline for future use.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Taking a corporate approach, it is quite normal that companies distribute dividends to shareholders after having posted positive results.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: We can frame our surplus distribution model vis-à-vis the dividend payout policy of a company.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: It is quite normal that a company makes a dividend payout to its shareholders amounting to 15% to 20% of net income.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Similarly, I think we can adopt the same approach in allocating the SG Bonus to our fellow Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: I believe this will serve the future, near term and now with the amounts of $6 billion, $2 billion and $1.6 billion from the total surplus of $9.6 billion.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: If this baseline model is reasonable, could this become a precedent to future surpluses as long as it is financially prudent to do so?

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: If yes, this will be in line with the Government's long-time commitment for sharing the fruits of the nation's development with fellow Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Instead, we need to build an ecosystem where the substantial part of giving is to be generated from the society itself.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: We need to find a way and establish a system which is sustainable, where giving has become a pleasure and giving is highly motivated.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: A system of recognition and reward should be explored in trying to encourage more giving.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: In a report in January 2017 made by SPD, formally known as the Society for the Physically Disabled, on the World Giving Index 2016, 140 countries across the globe were surveyed in 2015.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: In most countries surveyed, 1,000 questionnaires were completed by a representative sample of individuals living across the country.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Respondents were asked if they had done the following in the past month: first, helped a stranger or someone they did not know who needed help; second, donated money to charity; third, volunteered their time to their organisation.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: In terms of donating money, Singapore was the 19th most generous country in 2016.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: I am certain this gesture is very much welcome by charities and organisations alike that depend on donations to fund their operations.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: They rely on these tax deductions as a way to encourage donors to donate to their organisations.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: I believe it is a significant quantum to donors which could make a difference between giving more or remaining as it is.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: The 250% tax deduction promotes the spirit of giving among Singaporeans and encourages them to play a part in contributing back to the society to help others in need.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: This can be seen by the increase in donations by $0.7 billion dollars between 2011 and 2015.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: While this increase is good and encouraging, is it enough?

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: My time with the non-profit organisations has shown me that a large injection of funds is sometimes needed, especially when initiatives and programmes need to be rolled out.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: The large cash outlay goes towards recruiting new staff, setting up new infrastructure, training existing staff and other expenses needed to kickstart a new programme.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: This need for a large amount of funds often cannot be solely supported by donations received from the public.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Rather, Government grants and large donations from foundations, philanthropies make the difference on whether a new programme can be launched and implemented effectively.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: As such, while a 250% tax deduction is appreciated by all, I am of the opinion that more can be done to make it more attractive, especially donors from the upper-income band.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: To encourage more Singaporeans to donate, I would like to suggest a model for progressive tax deduction for donors which will take on a similar approach to the progressive tax imputation on our income received.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: This proposal will mean that instead of a flat rate of 250% for all donations, the tax deduction rate increases with a quantum of donation given.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Much like how incomes are broken down to bands to compute income tax rates, the same can be done for donations.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Chairman, let me first declare my interest as the advisor for the National Private Hire Vehicles Association.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Unlike previously, these drivers are now required to obtain a Land Transport Authority (LTA) Private Hire Car Driver’s Vocational Licence (PDVL) to provide point-to-point ride services.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: PHV drivers can only serve commuters who book their trips through the apps.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: All trips completed are also recorded, making it possible to identify the time spent providing hire-for-reward services from other usage.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: A full-time taxi hirer, in comparison, will have to achieve about 20 revenue trips per day to cover his costs and some take-home income for the day.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: A private hire driver may do fewer revenue trips as their consumer base is limited due to the fact that they only take trips based on what is assigned by the system.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Prior to LTA requiring all PHV drivers to obtain a licence, they were required to register a transport company, and this took care of the tax.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: In my view, the answer provided does not seem to clarify the circumstance well.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: How does not allowing PHV drivers claim tax deduction correlate to restriction of car population?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Is the Certificate of Entitlement (COE) scheme not already there to regulate the car population?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The service provided by private hire cars complements our public transport services and, anecdotally, I can say, to a certain extent, this service contributes to reducing the number of car ownership rather than increasing it.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I say so because I have friends who did not extend or buy new cars after their cars' COEs expired.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Reasons are that it is more convenient and cheaper to travel by private hire car as compared to owning one.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Mr Chairman, public communication on the way water is priced can be significantly improved.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: At last year's Budget Debate, the Minister in charge of the Ministry of the Environment and Water Resources (MEWR) shared that the numbers in the books of the Public Utilities Board (PUB) do not lend themselves to a straightforward understanding of what they mean.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Minister observed that while PUB's books are in accruals, the Ministry's Budget is in cash.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Minister also said that he would ask the Minister of Finance to look at a whole-of-Government approach to funding Singapore's water infrastructure because things do not add up if one looks at the books separately.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In light of these remarks, can I clarify what progress has been made on this?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Many Singaporeans note that PUB's books record significant surpluses after Government grants and that any increase in water prices should take into account the size of such surpluses.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: More fundamentally, there is a greater desire to understand the variables and assumptions that go into calculating Long Run Marginal Cost (LRMC), which forms the basis of determining water prices.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Under such a cash accounting convention, capital and operating budgets are lumped together, even though there is a great difference between capital investments and recurrent operating expenses.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: The recurrent operating expenses include items like administrative expenses, facility rentals and operations.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: This group of expenses tends to be sticky and, if not well-controlled, could be difficult to dial back.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Capital investments, on the other hand, is forward-looking and, if invested wisely, can yield significant returns in the future.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: In fact, under investments, Capital Expenditure may also be bad, as opportunities to reap future benefits may be missed out.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Therefore, I would like to ask the Minister if he could share with us the split between capital and recurrent expenses, and how has this ratio shifted over the years.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: In crafting the Budget, which is a strategic fiscal tool as the Minister pointed out, really is not just simple arithmetic.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: I think the Minister has to carefully balance many, many dimensions, sometimes, conflicting objectives.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: I can think of several: growing an economy through an expansionary Budget so as to grow the base but be careful not to overheat the economy for cost inflation; meeting the demands for funding all meritorious causes that can be sustained; meeting the needs of this generation and future generations; helping those who are in need without eroding our work ethos; and creating a fairer income distribution system yet having a competitive tax rate so that talents and enterprises do not flee this country.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: These are very difficult and complex issues requiring a lot of judgement, adroitness and so forth.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Chairman, value is not just about what we spend today, especially when it comes to fixed assets like construction projects and infrastructure.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: When we construct new Mass Rapid Transit (MRT) tunnels, the tender analysis should look at the designs and ask if it is easy to organise track access for maintenance.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Every minute counts when it comes to track access, as we have learnt over the years and recently.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Likewise, when we design and build a new HDB block, we should also ask whether it is easy to maintain the exterior facade.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: This includes little details, like whether horizontal struts are needed because such high-rise horizontal beams can be difficult to clean.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: This also means understanding human nature when buildings are designed.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: For example, high-rise littering still happens in many housing estates.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: In Clementi where I serve, some of the newer HDB blocks were reported to have so-called "award-winning designs".

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: These designs look very nice from afar, but some of these designs also very easily accumulate high-rise litter.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Chairman, when the building design makes it harder to maintain the exterior, when it becomes harder to keep the building clean, the costs do not go away.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: In the case of HDB blocks, the costs are passed on to the Town Council and, indirectly, passed on from there to the residents.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We can also require space in public buildings to be adaptable, so that as land needs change, a building can be repurposed without having to demolish or rebuild.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We can call it "building in prudence", "prudence by design".

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Chairman, I understand our need to have more spending in the years ahead.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: However, before we ask for more tax dollars from our people, we have a responsibility to them to ensure that we have done our best to remain prudent and ensure value-for-money in Government expenses.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Government share on what internal systems and controls will help us achieve this?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Government also share concrete examples of how savings have been achieved?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Having said that, it is important that in our drive for economy, we do not automatically go for the lowest bid in public tender, at the sacrifice of quality and long-term cost control, as per what fellow Member Dr Tan Wu Meng has just shared.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: It is also important that we do not pass the cost unnecessarily to the private sector and our people through unnecessary or over-complex regulations.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Government also share how we can best manage this important balance between economy and quality?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Chairman, with Government expenditure set to rise due to infrastructure renewal and building up of healthcare facilities, I hope that apart from having gateways to review the costing and design of large projects, that the Ministry can look into the processes that guide day-to-day Government procurement or assets.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: For instance, can we use centralised procurement to a larger extent to leverage economies of scale and get a better deal from suppliers?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Can the Ministries actively push for product standardisation and demand aggregation to ensure that we do not get creamed off by suppliers?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We could end up being charged different prices across different institutions for similar products if we are not careful.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Also, how do we ensure that purchase contracts best take care of our interests?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Are there specialised teams with technical knowledge of these assets to make a reasoned assessment of the costs?

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In the past, I have brought up the issue of high foreign worker levy for the sector.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I also filed a Parliamentary Question (PQ) on compliance costs for construction companies to implement various workplace safety requirements.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah also raised this issue during the Committee of Supply (COS) for the Ministry of Trade and Industry (MTI) last Friday.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I asked him why would the foreign companies tender at a price that they do not make any profits?

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: First, some of these firms have ambitions to be global construction players so they want to build up their track record, and winning a Government tender in Singapore will be seen as a feather in the cap.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Another reason is that, at the working level, the management team of such foreign-owned companies, and possibly their family members as well, may be comfortable staying in Singapore, and if they do not win the tender for major projects, they may be sent home.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Without winning the contracts in Singapore, they also find it difficult to build up a track record to compete overseas.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Chairman, for our national security reasons, I think it is important that we maintain a certain number of local construction companies.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As such, I hope MOF can take the above feedback into consideration in the award of Government tenders.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Chairman, Sir, in Budget 2016, the National Trade Platform (NTP) was announced and subsequently implemented in 2017.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: NTP was designed as an open innovation platform which businesses and service providers can tap on to develop new applications to support evolving business needs.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: As digitalisation continues to be a driver in our economy, NTP can become a showcase of how we can enable productivity improvements through streamlining digital information exchange.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: With the many ideas provided by industry stakeholders during this development, what are some further collaborations that MOF is undertaking with the private sector to co-create solutions for our businesses?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Conceptually, NTP is an attractive one-stop trade portal for Business-to-Government and Business-to-Business services.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: On the back of a thriving e-commerce landscape and Singapore being a key trading hub, are there any plans to expand this platform for other trade opportunities beyond customs and logistics?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: How can the platform developers or sector players continue to provide inputs for future frameworks?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, we are moving very swiftly on the use of information technology (IT) in our service delivery.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: From across all sectors, be it transport, retail, healthcare and finance, time and again, we see new apps being introduced, new online services and so forth to make services more hassle-free and it means cutting down waiting time and so on.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is a massive effort that the Civil Service has embarked on and will impact across the whole spectrum of our society.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The landing page of a Ministry's website or Statutory Board, for example, becomes the first line of contact with the public more so than the officers who sit behind the frontline counter.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: All these are part of our move towards a Smart Nation and moving to technology, and in how we can enhance citizen experience with technology.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Can the Minister for Finance give an update on how the Ministry and the Statutory Boards under its wings, such as IRAS and the Accounting and Corporate Regulatory Authority (ACRA), for example, are improving their service delivery to citizens and businesses through digitalisation?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How is the Government making better use of technology and improving processes to make timely payments to the individuals and businesses, which is an important part as it may help the cash flow to the recipients or businesses?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Can the Minister give an overview of MOF's digitalisation efforts as part of the Smart Nation drive?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How is the Public Service becoming more future-ready and tapping on technology to better serve the needs of our people and businesses?

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Mr Chairman, I thank the Members for their comments and questions for MOF.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Members’ questions covered four areas: first, our fiscal position, and our financing and surplus-sharing approach; second, the Government’s efforts in ensuring value-for-money in our spending and procurement; third, our plans to create opportunities for businesses and enhance citizen experience with technology; and fourth, the role of shareholders and some tax-related matters.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, I will address the cuts on the first two topics, and the Senior Minister of State Ms Indranee Rajah will take the other cuts.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: On our fiscal position, Mr Cedric Foo asked about the proportion of capital investment compared to recurrent spending or operating expenditure.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: One example that we are looking at is Changi Airport Terminal 5.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: If we do not do this, if we are not careful and selective in borrowing, we may end up over-burdening ourselves with rising interest costs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And that is not what we intend to do.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, therefore, even as we borrow, there will still be capital projects that we continue to fund through development expenditure from the annual Budget.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: It is slightly higher than what it used to be, but it is in the ballpark.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Looking ahead, we expect development expenditures to rise as we continue to invest in more capital projects.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But at the same time, operating expenditures are also going to increase, especially in areas that were highlighted in the Budget, like healthcare, security and other social spending.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, overall, both will go up, but we expect the share of development spending to continue to rise slightly in the coming years.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We will continue to monitor this share between operating and development spending.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Because if we spend too much on recurrent, then we are not investing enough for the future, not building capabilities for the future.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: If we spend too much on capital, then we may end up with a long tail of future spending for maintenance and replacement.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, it is critical to get the balance right, and that is what we are doing.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Many of the capital projects in the Government are undertaken by our Statutory Boards.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Mr Pritam Singh asked about the harmonisation of accounts because our Statutory Boards use the accrual basis for their accounts and the Ministries use cash.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This is the approach we have taken because we believe that cash accounting allows for better control of spending, and it is a more prudent way of fiscal management.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Many governments also do cash accounting for their Ministries.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But for statutory boards, they use accrual for their accounts because statutory boards are set up as separate legal entities with their own financial accounts.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Some statutory boards even go to the markets to borrow.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, we want our Statutory Boards to be subject to the same discipline as the private sector, and that is why they use accrual accounts, like what private sector companies do.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Regardless of whether the work is carried out by a Ministry or a Statutory Board, we take a whole-of-Government approach on how we finance our infrastructure.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The water network is a case in point.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Briefly put, PUB collects revenue and pays for the investment and operations and maintenance of the water supply system.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: That includes our reservoirs, treatment plants and pipelines and also the water reclamation plants for the treatment of used water.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: If there are any surpluses in its accounts, PUB will plough them back into investments in infrastructural works, such as the upgrading of waterworks, water reclamation plant expansions and investment in water treatment processes, as well as in research and development (R&D).

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And because there is this gap in its financing cash flows, PUB borrows for its capital investments.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, this is what happens within the PUB accounts.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: On top of this, the Government funds the drainage system that helps to manage flooding risks, the sewerage network system that helps to safeguard public health, and projects to help strengthen the resilience of our water supply.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: These assets are part of our total water loop, but they also provide benefits to all citizens.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, the Government pays for these assets and we do not recover the cost directly from consumers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Indeed, from FY2012 to FY2016, Government investments in drainage and sewerage totalled $2.1 billion, far in excess of the Water Conservation Tax revenue.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In the next decade, we are also building Phase 2 of the Deep Tunnel Sewerage System, which costs more than $4 billion.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: These are costly but important investments that we need to make.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: While they use different bases for accounting, as I have explained, each is appropriate for its use.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: What remains important is sound fiscal and financial management to ensure timely and adequate investments in our public infrastructure and assets.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We do this for water; we do this for all other public infrastructure as well.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Several Members ‒ Mr Liang Eng Hwa, Ms Foo Mee Har, Dr Tan Wu Meng, Mr Henry Kwek and Ms Sun Xueling ‒ spoke about the need to be prudent, efficient and effective in our spending.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This is, indeed, an area of continuing emphasis for MOF.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: I was a budget officer in MOF way back in 2000.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, I have seen first-hand how our budgeting system has evolved over the years.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Even back then, we had robust processes in place for budgeting.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We checked against cost norms, we made the necessary cuts in the budget of Ministries and agencies.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: It is not work that endears ourselves to colleagues in other Ministries, I assure you.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: They see MOF as blocking or delaying their projects.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But we take these in our stride and we do the work.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Now, almost 20 years later, I can say that our processes for budgeting and ensuring value-for-money have developed further and become even more rigorous.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We have put in place various systems and controls to ensure that our monies are spent effectively.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: First, the Block Budget Framework sets a spending limit for Ministries.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Within the budget given to them, each agency optimises its spending and channels resources to worthwhile programmes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We have the Budget Utilisation Framework which encourages Ministries to budget as closely as possible to their expenditure needs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This is to ensure that they do not set aside more than they require and, as a result, deprive other meritorious needs of funding.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But I would assure Ms Foo Mee Har that Ministries do not spend for the sake of spending or meeting the budget, especially during the end of the year.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: If there is under-utilisation of the budget due to reasons which are beyond the Ministries' control, there will not be reductions to their future budgets.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We also have mechanisms to give Ministries budgeting flexibility so they can roll over part of the savings from the operating budget to the next financial year.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: On top of all these, we conduct regular reviews of Ministries' budgets to make sure that they continue to be right-sized and ensure that every Ministry uses its allocated resources effectively and efficiently.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This is something that we have shared in this House.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: It is a rigorous multi-stage process that scrutinises the requirements, scope and design of the projects at key milestones before funding approval is given.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This process includes reviews not just by senior public officers, but by academics and industry practitioners where necessary, especially practitioners with deep technical expertise.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: These best practices, guidelines and case studies from the reviews are shared across the Public Service.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Fourth, the performance of key programmes are published by the Ministries for their respective areas.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: These performance indicators are also consolidated and reported in the Annual Revenue and Expenditure Estimates and in the Singapore Public Sector Outcomes Review, which is published once every two years.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Ms Foo Mee Har asked if agencies conduct productivity reviews to ensure their operating efficiency.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This framework allows for manpower to be redeployed to implement new programmes or deliver enhanced services, while preventing the over-expansion of public sector manpower over time.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Mr Liang Eng Hwa and some Members were concerned that the economy drive will impact on public services.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Even with the announced measures to constrain expenditure growth, overall Ministry budgets in dollar terms are still expected to grow, albeit at a slower rate.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Agencies are given time to adjust to the budget changes and will have the resources to fulfil their missions and maintain service levels.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Of course, achieving value-for-money goes beyond cutting costs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: It is also about creating greater value while we carefully manage the costs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Government agencies have sought to achieve value-for-money while improving service delivery and outcomes in various ways.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For infrastructure, in particular, something that Ms Foo Mee Har, Dr Tan Wu Meng and several others spoke about, we have stepped up efforts to manage our infrastructure spending.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: First, we adopt a systems approach when we plan and design projects.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We do not look at each project in isolation, but we consider how they affect one another, and the potential synergies of multiple projects collectively.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We look for opportunities for infrastructure integration, which allows us to achieve better outcomes or reap savings.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Another example is the integration of PUB’s Tuas Water Reclamation Plant with NEA's Integrated Waste Management Facility which brings about a number of synergies while optimising land use.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This allows both facilities to be self-sufficient in energy.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The two plants will also enjoy other synergies, like the sharing of common administrative facilities.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: It creates more value, maximises synergies and that is what we are doing.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: It also allows us to take a lifecycle perspective when planning and designing our infrastructure, which several Members spoke about as well.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Dr Tan Wu Meng and Ms Sun Xueling highlighted the need to ensure value-for-money over the lifecycle of our infrastructure.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This is, indeed, an area we are placing greater emphasis on.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We typically associate architects and designers with aesthetics and they do produce very beautiful buildings.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But I think the architectural profession, too, is very conscious that they cannot just design for aesthetics.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: They also have to design for functionality and maintainability, and that shift is happening.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The Building and Construction Authority (BCA) issues guides to help architects and designers better understand how they can design public buildings to achieve safer, more labour-efficient and more cost-effective maintenance downstream.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: BCA is also helping the industry and the architectural profession to make this shift towards better designs for functionality and maintainability.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Public sector agencies, like HDB and JTC, have incorporated these guidelines into their checklist when they do procurement and projects.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, Members will see a lot more consciousness in lifecycle considerations and in good design when these projects are being done.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: With a lifecycle approach, we do not just look at the upfront price of a project but we look at the overall lifecycle cost.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, it makes sense from a lifecycle cost perspective.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Apart from such efforts, we are building up core engineering capabilities within the Government, as highlighted by Ms Sun Xueling, to achieve value-for-money for public projects from a lifecycle perspective.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The Centre of Excellence for Building and Infrastructure was set up in 2016 under JTC.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This is a shared service centre to help build and sustain inhouse engineering capabilities across the Public Service, from planning, design, project management to facilities management.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: One example is JTC's efforts to roll out smart facilities management solutions for its industrial properties.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: By monitoring and analysing real-time data from its buildings centrally, JTC is able to better optimise building performance and respond to faults quickly.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: JTC is sharing its experiences and lessons learnt with the rest of the public sector.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: To maximise value from limited resources, Government agencies also look for new and innovative ways to "do more with less".

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We continue to challenge the status quo and make use of technology to enhance work effectiveness while achieving manpower savings.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: I am sure many Members would have heard about this or are already using it today.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We have been trying to do away with parking coupons for some time.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The original thinking was that this could be achieved through Electronic Road Pricing (ERP) 2.0, but this would have taken some time and it would have been a very complex system.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Last year, a team of the Government Technology Agency (GovTech), HDB and Urban Renewal Authority (URA) officers came together to develop the Parking.sg app.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We now have a quick and convenient way to pay for short-term parking.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Drivers are only charged on a per-minute basis and they can extend their parking sessions remotely, instead of having to return to their vehicles to add more coupons.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Delivering value for every dollar spent is the responsibility of each and every Public Service officer.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But it should not be limited to Government agencies alone.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Through greater partnership with businesses and the community, we have worked hand in hand to deliver better outcomes for Singapore and Singaporeans.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: One example is IRAS' hackathon to crowdsource solutions to make it an easier experience for companies and individuals to file their taxes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But we can make the process streamlined and convenient for everyone.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: A group of individuals, who called themselves TinkerTax was one of the winners in the hackathon.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: It is an online application that helps small and medium enterprises (SMEs) prepare for the submission of their corporate income tax returns.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: With TinkerTax, companies can convert accounting income to taxable income for their income tax returns in three easy steps.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This innovative solution helps small companies as it allows them to complete their tax return filing more easily.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Our libraries are also a good example of partnering the community to encourage everyone to contribute towards a shared journey of lifelong learning.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Volunteer-run spaces in libraries have increased by over 300% in the past three years.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For example, an entire floor of the Tampines Regional Library is run by volunteers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: There is also a dedicated library space for volunteers to gather and plan activities to promote reading to other library users.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Together with the re-engineering of its library spaces and services to introduce more automation and self-service, the National Library Board (NLB) has been able to increase its staff productivity.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Ms Sun Xueling and Mr Henry Kwek raised important points about ensuring value-for-money in our procurement, and I will explain our approach to achieving this.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Every agency procures through a central procurement portal, the Government Electronic Business (GeBIZ), and most suppliers submit invoices electronically through a platform called Vendors@Gov.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This allows Government agencies and suppliers to reap efficiency gains.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: There is a perception out there that Government purchases only on price alone.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Quality factors would include reliability, innovativeness, expertise of the vendor, track record and much more.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For construction-related tenders, which make up more than half of our annual procurement value, BCA has enhanced the frameworks to place even greater emphasis on quality from this year onwards.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For example, consultancy tenderers are now required to provide a breakdown of the manpower deployment and rates, so that agencies can better assess whether the proposed resources commensurate with the quoted fees.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: BCA has also introduced consultants' and contractors' past performance as a mandatory criterion for tender evaluation.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This provides a quality feedback loop to recognise firms that have performed well in previous projects.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Thirdly, the public sector seeks to centralise our procurement wherever appropriate.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: One way is by aggregating demand for common purchases across agencies.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: One agency calls a bulk tender on behalf of others.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This minimises administration costs and enables quantity discounts.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The commonly-purchased categories include office equipment, graphic design, travel-related services, and infocomm-related products and services ‒ all on bulk tender.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: There is, however, a limit to how much centralisation or standardisation is optimal.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For example, we risk vendor capture if many agencies buy from a single supplier and we are locked in to the same supplier for subsequent maintenance and replacements.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We also need to be mindful of providing sufficient opportunities for SMEs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Indeed, many Members often ask about giving more opportunities for small firms to bid for Government projects.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: If we have too large a contract, it is more likely to be taken up by the big suppliers only.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Too much centralisation or standardising also limits flexibilities or variations to meet the unique needs of agencies or situations.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, we need to strike a judicious balance.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We are stepping up procurement training for our officers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We have partnered the Singapore University of Social Sciences (SUSS) and the Defence Science and Technology Agency (DSTA) for this purpose.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Lead agencies with deep procurement capabilities are providing advice and solutions to the rest of the public sector.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We are also building up capabilities to enable negotiations to be carried out in a fair way that achieves value-for-money and win-win outcomes for both buyers and suppliers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Mr Yee Chia Hsing asked about the support for the local construction sector.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Actually, this cut may be better filed under the Ministry of National Development (MND).

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: I am not sure if I am taking this as MOF or MND.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We can discuss further in the MND COS coming up later.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Mr Yee asked if we can require foreign companies to form a joint venture with local firms to bid for our construction contracts.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We are aware that this happens, but it is not limited to foreign firms.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The fact is that the construction industry is in a downturn.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Many companies are bidding for projects and there is price-diving.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But, as I have highlighted earlier, price is not the only factor used in evaluating Government tenders.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We are placing greater emphasis on the quality factors.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We have also introduced measures to deter "price-diving" because we want to avoid the situation where a company, local or foreign, tries too hard to secure a contract, dives the prices and then ends up not being able to deliver, or worse, compromise on quality just to get the project done within that price.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, for construction tenders, various agencies have adopted practices to identify abnormally low bids and scrutinise the contractors' ability to deliver the projects at such prices.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We also continue to ensure our construction contracts remain accessible to local companies that may be smaller in size.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Where suitable, we have broken up some of our bigger projects into smaller contracts, to give local companies a better opportunity to participate.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Encouragingly, some local companies are also partnering foreign companies to undertake bigger projects, not by mandating it, but they are voluntarily doing so, like Woh Hup, which has been partnering Shanghai Tunnel Engineering to construct an MRT line and station.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: There will be technology transfer in future so that our local firms can bid for these projects on their own.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Our approach is not to restrict competition but help our companies level up their capabilities so that they are competitive on their own merits.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: These premium subsidies for lower- and middle-income Singaporeans will ensure that the enhanced ElderShield scheme remains affordable, and the premium subsidies will directly benefit individuals and families.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, you have to look at the surplus in totality.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We give them all back to Singaporeans, but we give back in different forms.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In fact, the support we provide to Singaporeans who need help goes beyond the SG Bonus and these direct transfer schemes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In various areas, like housing, healthcare, education and childcare, we have enhanced the support provided by our permanent schemes over the years with more assistance targeted at the lower-income.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Mr Chairman, against the backdrop of rising needs, the Government will continue to fund our expenditure wisely and manage our spending prudently.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We will ensure that our policies and processes for budgeting, procurement and evaluation, help us to optimise resources and achieve value-for-money.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We will partner the private sector and the community to create a better future for Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Mr Chairman, let me address Members' questions on creating opportunities for businesses, enhancing citizen experience with technology and the Government's position on corporate governance and tax-related matters.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Miss Cheryl Chan asked how MOF is collaborating with the private sector to co-create solutions for businesses.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In line with this Budget's thrust to build a vibrant and innovative economy, Government agencies, including MOF, continue to partner businesses, trade associations, unions and overseas government regulators to deepen international connectivity and strengthen enterprise capabilities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: First, is NTP, which Miss Cheryl Chan asked about.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This is a one-stop platform spearheaded by Singapore Customs, with support from MTI, GovTech and the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), among others.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: It incorporates existing TradeNet and TradeXchange systems, synergising business-to-government (B2G) and business-to-business (B2B) processes, while introducing new services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The NTP enables trade and logistics businesses to share and reuse data and documents faster and more securely between partners and the Government.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This end-to-end digitisation of trade documents and processes will increase business productivity, improve process efficiency, and strengthen mutual trust across the trade value chain.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This first phase involves working with commercial providers to offer value-added services that go beyond customs and logistics.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: These include service solutions in supply chain financing and trade news.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: One such example is Nufin Data's New Efficiencies More Options (NEMO), a cloud-based supply chain financing solution which helps traders boost their cash flows by connecting buyers, suppliers and funders to turn trade receivables and payables faster into free cash flow.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: More services will be rolled out in the coming months.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We welcome collaboration and will continue to engage the various stakeholders to innovate and keep the services offered vibrant.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Together with design thinking consultants and DesignSingapore, we have engaged companies to identify areas where new services could be created to support their trade digitisation journey.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We also have a developer sandbox which will release specific Application Programming Interfaces (APIs) and data to interested developers to tinker and come up with innovative service offerings.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We are also working with overseas partners to make cross-border trade cheaper, safer and more efficient.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: These tie-ups will give businesses access to their regional and global partners.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: An example is the Global Trade Connectivity Network that will use distributed ledger technology, which is the technology behind block chains, to build an information highway between NTP and the Hong Kong Trade Finance Platform.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Second, the Association of Small and Medium Enterprises (ASME), with support from the Standards, Productivity and Innovation Board (SPRING) Singapore, ACRA and IRAS, has developed the SME Cloud Exchange Network software.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This partnership aims to increase SMEs’ productivity by offering them accounting and human resource (HR) solutions to help them file returns to ACRA, IRAS and Central Provident Fund (CPF) Board.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The Government will continue to work closely with trade associations to accelerate the pace of digital adoption and raise productivity of our SMEs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Third, IRAS’ API marketplace allows anyone to develop applications that interface seamlessly with IRAS' systems.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This is a significant move taken by IRAS to open up its interfaces to facilitate business and productivity solutions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: JustLogin and Sage Software Asia are two local enterprises that have incorporated IRAS’ Auto-Inclusion Scheme API into their payroll software.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This allows employers to submit their employees' income data directly to IRAS via the vendors' payroll software.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: For 2018, IRAS has worked with 45 other payroll software vendors to benefit many more employers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This will raise efficiency and effectiveness across the industry.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Such collaboration allows innovative solutions to be developed by the private sector or the community.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We encourage more of such efforts to co-create business solutions with the Government.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The Government will continue to harness technology to help save citizens' time and effort, as well as provide faster responses and payments to them.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat asked for an update and an overview of how MOF is enhancing citizen experience with technology under the Smart Nation Drive.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: To ensure greater convenience for companies, ACRA will be simplifying the filing of annual returns for exempt private companies and private dormant relevant companies in 2018.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: ACRA will also be providing the simplified filing service on its "ACRA On The Go" mobile app, so that filing by these companies can now be done anytime and anywhere.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: To make it even more convenient when it is time to file, companies will be prompted by a short message service (SMS) with a link to the mobile app.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: With over 30,000 companies incorporated each year, some new companies may not be familiar with their corporate tax obligations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This interactive kit provides tailored information, such as tax-filing timeline and follow-up actions, and automatically sends email notifications with reminders on filing due dates.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat also asked how the Government is making better use of technology and improving processes to make timely payments to businesses and individuals.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: First, we have moved towards SMS notifications for the GST Voucher (GSTV).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Second, the Accountant-General’s Department (AGD), together with the Public Service Division (PSD), the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) and MOE, introduced the PaC@Gov mobile app for public officers in 2017.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This enables common staff transactions, such as leave and claims to be carried out anytime, anywhere.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Since the launch, more than 50% of our officers using PaC@Gov have downloaded the mobile app and more than 400,000 transactions have been carried out through the app in the past year.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Third, we understand the importance of cash flow to businesses.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The Government processes an average of two million payments to more than 23,000 companies annually.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We target to bring down the late payment rate below 5%, in other words, to achieve at least 95% of timely payment to businesses.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We are working to automate the procurement-to-payment process, which will enable faster payments to businesses.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We encourage businesses to issue electronic invoices when providing goods and services to the Government.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: A paperless and more efficient processing will result in faster payments to vendors.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: From 2018, all businesses that transact with the Government only need to submit their payment details once.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Businesses do not have to submit their payment details every time they transact with a different Government agency.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: They can also use the Vendors@Gov mobile app to track their payment status anytime, anywhere.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: I move now to the issue of Governance.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Mr Leon Perera and Ms Sylvia Lim asked about the roles played by Temasek and GIC in relation to their investee companies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Ms Sylvia Lim also asked what role Temasek can play in promoting ethical behaviour in the entities that Temasek invests in.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Both made a reference to the Santiago Principles.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: I should mention that GIC was one of the founding participants of the International Forum of Sovereign Wealth Funds that came up with the Santiago Principles.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Before I address what GIC and Temasek do, I think it will be helpful if I just restate, once again, the legal position with respect to shareholders and companies, so that we all know the framework that we are talking about.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Under company law, the shareholders of a company have certain powers, which is to appoint and remove boards, and to have a statutory right to the audited financial statements of the company.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: However, shareholders do not interfere in the business decisions or operations of its portfolio companies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: These are the responsibilities of the respective companies’ boards and management.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Temasek and GIC are shareholders of their investee companies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: So, they hold the boards of their investee companies responsible for conducting their affairs properly and delivering sustainable returns over the long term.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Mr Leon Perera then asked – he understands, of course, that I said that Temasek and GIC do not interfere with the management of the companies – does that mean that they are truly hands-off?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Well, it depends on what he means by "hands-off".

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: If by "hands-off", he is asking do they interfere or get involved in/with the day-to-day management and operation decisions of the companies, then of course, no, because that goes against the general principle of how companies are set up.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Shareholders should not really be jumping into the day-to-day management; that is left to the Boards.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: But if Mr Perera's question is: do they engage with investee companies, share ideas, talk to them generally about broad topics and investment things, then the answer is yes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: GICs' investment teams engage the management teams of their portfolio companies to encourage policies and business practices that support sustainable long-term financial performance.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
